A row that is not mounted yet renders a placeholder with an estimated height. A row mounts when it gets close to the viewport. An IntersectionObserver watches its placeholder, with the edit view's scroll container as root. The other rows mount in the background, one per idle period (requestIdleCallback, inside startTransition so that user input interrupts it). A row with a field in error mounts right away, so the error is displayed and the field can receive the focus. It stays mounted after the errors are cleared. A row with a required UID or a custom field mounts with the page, including when the field is inside a non-repeatable component. These inputs can set a value when they mount: a required UID fetches its default value, and a custom field may set a default. Once mounted, a row stays mounted. Relation fields follow the same idea for their requests. A relation field fetches its connected relations once it gets close to the viewport (useHasBeenNearViewport, same margin as the rows), not when it mounts, and searches for the options of its combobox only once the combobox has been opened. After a save, only the fields that have already been near the viewport refetch their relations. A field in a row that is not mounted yet is not in the DOM. This affects browser search, autofill, end-to-end tests that look for a field low in the form without scrolling, and plugins that query inputs in the DOM. The form values do not depend on mounting: they live in the form state.

Because the list view is essentially a giant table, its data-structure is considerably simpler than the edit view: interface ListFieldLayout { /** * The attribute data from the content-type's schema for the field */ attribute: Attribute.Any | { type: 'custom' }; // custom attributes are expected to use `cellFormatter`. /** * Typically used by plugins to render a custom cell */ cellFormatter?: ( data: { [key: string]: unknown }, header: Omit<ListFieldLayout, 'cellFormatter'>, meta: { collectionType: string; model: string } ) => React.ReactNode; label: string | MessageDescriptor; /** * the name of the attribute we use to display the actual name e.g. relations * are just ids, so we use the mainField to display something meaninginful by * looking at the target's schema */ mainField?: string; name: string; searchable?: boolean; sortable?: boolean; } The cellFormatter property is paramount to plugin developers being able to inject their own columns, because we, most likely, will not have the components necessary to render the data the plugin provides. This is why they receive the data for the entire row & the header that they injected via the 'Admin/CM/pages/ListView/inject-column-in-table' hook. The third argument, meta, holds the collectionType and model of the list view. Its type is exported as ListCellMeta from @strapi/content-manager/strapi-admin. :::caution Pass fields, never spread the row The row is user data. A content type can have attributes named ref or key. React treats them as the special ref and key props when you spread the row into a component: a string ref crashes the list view ("Function components cannot have string refs") and key is dropped. Read the fields your cell needs and pass them explicitly: cellFormatter: (row, _header, { model }) => <MyCell documentId={row.documentId} model={model} />; :::
The live preview feature lets users see their content rendered on their frontend while editing. It includes visual editing that identifies and highlights editable fields.

Visual editing requires running some of our code on the user's frontend to detect fields and draw highlights. The obvious approach would be an SDK package users install in their project. We intentionally avoided this. An SDK would require ongoing maintenance and create version mismatch risks between the SDK and Strapi. It would also tie us to specific frameworks or require multiple framework-specific packages. Instead, the preview script is defined inside Strapi and sent to the frontend via postMessage. The frontend just needs a small snippet to receive and execute it. This keeps the script always in sync with the CMS version, works with any framework, and requires no package installation.

The preview script (packages/core/content-manager/server/src/preview/controllers/previewScript.js) is served verbatim from a server endpoint (GET /content-manager/preview/script). The admin fetches it, wraps it with its runtime config, and posts the result to the iframe: const previewScriptSource = await fetch( `${window.strapi.backendURL}/content-manager/preview/script` ).then((res) => res.text()); const config = { colors: previewHighlightColors, events: INTERNAL_EVENTS, parentOrigin: window.location.origin, }; const script = `(${previewScriptSource})(${JSON.stringify(config)})`; Because of this, it cannot import dependencies or reference external variables. All logic must be self-contained. The only external code (@vercel/stega for decoding) is loaded dynamically from a CDN at runtime. It lives in a standalone .js file served as-is rather than being bundled with the admin: a bundler wraps the module in helper code that breaks once the function is stringified and injected into the iframe. The file is still type-checked via @ts-check and JSDoc. This is why the file has an unusual structure with many functions defined inline.

We use stega encoding to identify which Strapi field each piece of text comes from. Stega embeds invisible metadata into text content using Unicode zero-width characters that are imperceptible to users but can be decoded programmatically. The Document Service encodes field metadata into text values (invisible to users) The frontend renders the content normally The preview script decodes the metadata and attaches data-strapi-source attributes to DOM elements Highlights are drawn over elements with source attributes The metadata uses URL search params format, because it makes it easy to encode and decode multiple pieces of information into a single string: path=title&type=string&documentId=abc123&locale=en&model=api::page.page

Stega can only encode strings. This means: Numbers and booleans aren't encoded — we can't modify their type in the response. Fields inside components and dynamic zones work — we encode individual string fields within them, not the parent object. The path includes indices (e.g., components.2.title) to identify the exact field. Media fields work partially — the string properties inside media objects (like url, name, alternativeText) get encoded when traversed. Blocks fields hold a JSON AST rather than a plain string, so they can't use the standard stega encoding. They use a dedicated path described in Blocks visual editing below.

The admin panel and preview iframe communicate via postMessage. Public events (previewReady, strapiScript, strapiUpdate, strapiFieldChange) are documented to users—changing them is a breaking change. Internal events (for field focus/blur synchronization) are defined in packages/core/content-manager/admin/src/preview/utils/constants.ts and can be changed freely since we control both ends.

Users can configure the preview behavior from their frontend via window globals, without modifying Strapi: window.STRAPI_DISABLE_STEGA_DECODING - disable field detection entirely. When true, users need to write the data-strapi-source attribute manually for fields to be editable window.STRAPI_HIGHLIGHT_HOVER_COLOR - customize hover highlight color window.STRAPI_HIGHLIGHT_ACTIVE_COLOR - customize active highlight color

Blocks fields hold a JSON AST, so their content can't use the stega string encoding that other field types rely on. They use a dedicated flow: the server encodes lightweight stega markers into the text leaves of the AST, and double-clicking the rendered field opens the regular InputPopover with the cursor pre-positioned at the clicked block.

The server-side content-source-maps service (packages/core/core/src/services/content-source-maps.ts) has a dedicated encodeBlocks pass over the blocks AST. Instead of encoding every text node, it injects one stega marker per visual block: paragraph, heading, and quote nodes: the first { type: 'text' } leaf in the subtree. list nodes: the first text leaf of each list item (recursively for nested lists). image nodes: the alternativeText string field, when non-empty (encoded into the alt attribute — the preview script decodes this to detect image blocks). The url field is intentionally not encoded because stega-encoding it corrupts the src attribute and can cause the preview highlight to expand across the full page. Image blocks with no alternativeText receive no stega marker; the blocks field is still highlightable via its text blocks. code blocks are skipped — encoding their content would corrupt the syntax. All markers within one blocks field share both the same fieldPath key (e.g., fieldPath=content) and the same path key — blocksFieldMetadata sets path = fieldPath for every marker. The presence of fieldPath in the source attribute is what distinguishes blocks markers from regular string-field markers, and the preview script uses it as the group key to cluster all markers into one highlight.

The deriveGroupKey function in the preview script detects the presence of fieldPath in a data-strapi-source attribute and strips path from the group key, so all encoded spans within one blocks field share a single HighlightGroup. The bounding box of that group is computed in computeGroupRect, via getBlocksContainer. getBlocksContainer trusts an already-established, still-attached container for the group without re-checking it — it only runs the guarded discovery below when there's no cached container yet. This matters because live edits can legitimately dwarf a field's currently-marked content (e.g. typing an image into a field whose only marked content is a short paragraph); re-validating on every redraw would otherwise reject the still-correct container and collapse the highlight. The cache is populated by syncContainerObservation (see Live container resize) and shared with findBlockIndex. Fresh discovery (findBlocksContainer), run only when there's no cached container: Walk up the DOM from the first span in the group looking for an ancestor whose direct children include a block-level tag (P, H1–H6, UL, OL, BLOCKQUOTE, PRE), skipping LI, UL, and OL elements themselves — a list item can have a nested <ul>/<ol> as a direct child (which would satisfy the check but is not the container), and @strapi/blocks-react-renderer places nested lists directly inside <ul>/<ol> rather than wrapped in an <li>, so list containers also need to be skipped as candidates. Reject the candidate if its area is more than MAX_CONTAINER_AREA_RATIO (6x) larger than the union of the group's own marked elements — this stops an image-only field (no block-level tags of its own) from escaping into an unrelated, page-level ancestor and swallowing the whole page. Use the container's getBoundingClientRect() as the highlight rect. This includes container padding and empty trailing blocks that have no stega spans. Fallback (if no container is found): union of all span rects plus an 80 px bottom buffer so that empty trailing blocks remain clickable.

Live edits never carry a stega tag until the field is saved, so growing or shrinking content inside an already-open blocks field (typing a new paragraph, adding an image) doesn't touch any marked span — nothing signals the highlight manager that a redraw is needed. syncContainerObservation covers this gap: whenever a group's container is (re)established, a shared containerResizeObserver (ResizeObserver) watches it, and any resize triggers updateAllHighlights(). containerResizeObserver is disconnected in __strapi_previewCleanup alongside the other observers. Since the preview script re-runs on every iframe navigation and strapiScript re-injection, leaving it connected would leak one live observer — still pinning its watched DOM node — per re-run.

Double-clicking a blocks field highlight opens the editor at the clicked block. The preview script picks the element at the click point via pickElementAtPoint, which reports whether it was an exact hit (inside a marked element's own rect) or a fallback to the nearest marked element (only good for "which field", not "which block"). Exact hit: findBlockIndex(anchor, groupKey, group) resolves the block index — it gets the field's container via getBlocksContainer, walks up from the clicked span until its parent is the container, and returns the DOM child index of that element. The full children list (not filtered by tag name) is used so that empty paragraphs (
) and other non-standard elements don't cause index drift. No exact hit: the click landed on something unmarked — a code block or alt-less image (never marked, by design), or content rendered from a live, unsaved edit (not marked yet, since nothing is stega-encoded until the field is saved). Either way, findBlockIndex doesn't actually need a marker — it only needs a genuine DOM descendant of the field container to walk up from. The script finds the real clicked element with document.elementsFromPoint (skipping past the highlight overlay itself, which is what actually received the click) and resolves its block index the same way as an exact hit. This is different from falling back to the nearest marked sibling (which is only reliable for "which field", not "which block", and is what the fallback anchor above is still used for — path/popover position, not block index). For the popover trigger position the script uses the clicked element's rect — not the full group rect — so the popover opens adjacent to the clicked line. If the stega span is zero-width (invisible chars only), it walks up to the nearest visible ancestor. strapiFieldFocusIntent is sent with the path set to the fieldPath value (the blocks field path) and blockIndex in the payload — a number, or null when it couldn't be resolved (see above). InputPopover receives the message and calls setPopoverField with both the field metadata and the blockIndex. InputPopoverProvider makes blockIndex available via usePreviewPopoverBlockIndex() to all inputs rendered inside the popover. InputRenderer picks up blockIndex and passes it — along with livePreviewSync={true} — to BlocksInput → BlocksEditor. BlocksEditor's blockIndex effect runs on mount: it calls Transforms.select(editor, Editor.start(editor, [targetIndex])) to position the Slate cursor (clamped to the last block if the index is out of range) and focuses the editor. Editor.start — rather than a literal [targetIndex, 0] path — resolves the actual first valid text point inside that block, which matters for blocks whose first child isn't a plain text leaf (list items, headings with nested inline formatting). A requestAnimationFrame callback then scrolls that block into view inside the editor's scroll container.

When a blocks field is rendered inside an InputPopover, InputRenderer passes livePreviewSync={true} to BlocksEditor. In this mode onChange fires synchronously on every Slate operation instead of being debounced by 300 ms. This keeps the form state current so that an immediate Save after typing doesn't lose the last few keystrokes. autoFocus is set to true only when blockIndex is null (i.e., the field was opened by clicking on an empty area with no block identified). When blockIndex is a number, the blockIndex effect handles both cursor positioning and focus.

Live-preview sync updates the iframe DOM while the popover is open (the host app re-renders its BlocksRenderer on each strapiFieldChange). This can change the rendered height of the blocks field, making the group highlight stale. When popoverField transitions from a non-null value back to null (the popover closed), Preview.tsx posts strapiRescanHighlights to the iframe. The preview script handles this message by scheduling highlightManager.rescan() via requestAnimationFrame, which: Prunes any data-strapi-source elements that were removed from the DOM during editing. Registers any new elements that appeared (e.g., newly created blocks). Redraws all highlight positions and sizes. The requestAnimationFrame delay lets any in-flight React renders in the iframe commit before the rescan runs.

While the popover is open, the admin fires strapiFieldChange on every keystroke. strapiFieldChange is a public event — its name is stable and host apps can depend on it without risk of a breaking change. The preview script re-dispatches it as a CustomEvent on the iframe window so host apps don't need to deal with the postMessage origin checks themselves: // Preferred: CustomEvent dispatched by the preview script on the iframe window window.addEventListener('strapiFieldChange', (e) => { const { field, value } = e.detail; // update your local state with the new blocks AST }); // Alternative: raw postMessage received in the iframe from the admin parent window.addEventListener('message', (e) => { if (e.data?.type === 'strapiFieldChange') { const { field, value } = e.data.payload; // update your local state with the new blocks AST } });
documents.s: Live update integration for host apps

documents.t: Relations are a term used to describe how two or more entities are connected. Previously in the sidebar of an entity, in Nov2020 we released a refactor that moved these fields into the main editing flow for a better editor experience and to improve performance of the CMS application when many relations were used. above: An example of the relations input in the CMS edit view
above: A high-level diagram of how relations state management works

When you first open an existing entity, we call the admin API and put the data into the store to pre-populate fields with existing values. However, its important to know when you have fields with type === 'relation' in your schema that the data you receive will not be an array, but rather an object with the count of how many relations in that field exist. For example, a section of the response may look like this: { "my_relations": { "count": 6 } } So without intervention, your inputs would try to append new relations to the my_relations object, which would not work. Instead of this, before calling the redux action INIT_FORM we recursively find the paths fields based on the following conditions: The field is a relation The field is a component The field is a repeatable component The field is a dynamic zone These paths do not take into account index values. So if you have a repeatable component field where the schema looks like: { "repeatable_single_component_relation": { "type": "component", "repeatable": true, "component": "basic.relation" } } and the components looks like: { "basic.relation": { "attributes": { "id": { "type": "integer" }, "categories": { "type": "relation", "relation": "oneToMany", "target": "api::category.category", "targetModel": "api::category.category", "relationType": "oneToMany" }, "my_name": { "type": "string" } } } } Then the path to the relation field would be repeatable_single_component_relation.categories. Even though when relations are added the path to the field in the redux store would be repeatable_single_component_relation.0.categories. Inside the reducer we reduce the array of relationalFieldPaths to an object with the initialValues clone as the base. If there is modifiedData in the browser i.e. you've made changes to the entity and saved those changes, we just replace the first level of the field with the modifiedData so the data structure is preserved and we're not losing the relations we had already loaded in the component. If the first part of the path is highlighted as the relationalField then we simply replace that initial object with an empty array. However, if the first part of the path is either a repeatable component, a dynamic zone or a regular component then we recursively find the relation fields and replace the object with an array. This is handled by the findLeafByPathAndReplace utility function. This function in short, takes an end path (in this case the relational field) and a primitive to replace when it finds the endpath (an empty array in this case). It then recursively reduces the paths to the relational field mapping through arrays if necessary (in the instance of repeatable components for example) replacing the endpath with the primitive. When this is done, we have successfully prepared our initial data for usage with relations.
documents.s: Preparing relation fields in the store

documents.t: Because we've prepared the fields prior to the component loading, adding & removing relations, it's relatively easy to do so. When a relation is added, we simply push the new relation to the array of relations. When a relation is removed, we simply filter out the relation from the array of relations. This is handled inside the reducer actions CONNECT_RELATION & DISCONNECT_RELATION respectively. note Connecting relations adds the item to the end of the list, whilst loading more relations prepends to the beginning of the list. This is the expected behaviour, to keep the order of the list in the UI in sync with the API response. The RelationInput component takes the field in modifiedData as its source of truth. You could therefore consider this to be the browserState and initialData to be the serverState. When relations are loaded they're added to both the initialData and modifiedData objects, but when you connect/disconnect only the modifiedData is updated. This is useful when we're preparing data for the API.

The API to update the entity expects relations to be categorised into two groups, a connect array and disconnect array. You could do this as the user interacts with the input but we found this to be confusing and then involved us managing three different arrays which makes the code more complex. Instead, because the browser doesn't really care about what's new and removed and we have a copy of the slice of data we're mutating from the server we can run a small diff algorithm to determine which relations have been connected and which have been disconnected. Returning an object like so: { "my_relations": { "connect": [{ "id": 1 }, { "id": 2 }], "disconnect": [] } }
documents.s: Cleaning data to be posted to the API

documents.t: The input field for relation fields consist of two components:

This container component handles data fetching and data normalization for the RelationInput component. This has been extracted from the RelationInput so that Strapi is able to move the underlying component into the design-system if the community would need it (most other input components can be consumed from there).

This component is the presentational counterpart to the RelationInputDataManager component. It renders an input field based on the data passed from the data manager. Under the hood it is using react-window to render a list of relations in a virtualized view. Some fields need to render thousands of relations, which would otherwise have a negative impact on the overall performance of the content-manager.

This hook takes care of data-fetching and normalizes results relations as well as search-results. const { relations: RelationResults, search: RelationResults, searchFor } = useRelation(reactQueryCacheKey: Array<string | object>, options: Options);

options is a mandatory configuration and should implement the following shape: type Options = { name: string; // name of the relation field relation: RelationConfiguration; search: SearchConfiguration; } type RelationConfiguration = { endpoint: string; // URL from where existing relations should be fetched enabled: boolean; // defines whether relations should be fetched once the hook is called pageParams: object; // additional query params which will be appended to `endpoint` onLoad: (results: RelationResult[]) => void; // callback that will be fired after relations have been fetched (paginated) normalizeArguments = { mainFieldName: string; // name of the target model main field, determining which field to display (fallback: id) shouldAddLink: boolean; // if the user is allowed to read the target model, the returned relations should include a link to the target targetModel: object; // target content-type model }; pageGoal: number; // the current page-count of the already loaded relations used to keep the redux store and query cache in sync. } type SearchConfiguration = { endpoint: string; // URL from where new relations should be fetched pageParams: object; // additional query params which will be appended to `endpoint` }

relations and search both return a consistent relation format: type RelationResults = RelationResult[]; type RelationResult = { id: number; href?: string; // based on `shouldAddLink` and the `targetModel` publicationState: 'draft' | 'published'; mainField: string; // will fallback to "id" if not set }; relations​ relations refers to a inifinite-query return type from react-query. It exposes paginated relational data as well as methods to check if there are more pages or fetch more paginated results. Relations for a given field are fetched as soon as the hook is called. search​ search refers to a inifinite-query return type from react-query. It exposes paginated search results for a relational field. Search results are only fetched after searchFor() has been called. searchFor(string)​ searchFor is a method which can be used to search for entities which haven't been connected with the source entity yet. The method accepts a search-term: searchFor("term").

The Permission Checker is a service in Strapi that helps enforce access control policies by verifying user permissions for various actions on content entities. It provides methods to check, sanitize, and validate user actions based on their permissions.

Permission Checking: Verify whether a user has the necessary permissions for a specific action. Sanitization: Remove unauthorized fields from input and output data. Validation: Ensure that queries and input data comply with permission rules. Query Enforcement: Modify queries to include permission constraints automatically.

The service defines the following actions: const ACTIONS = { read: 'plugin::content-manager.explorer.read', create: 'plugin::content-manager.explorer.create', update: 'plugin::content-manager.explorer.update', delete: 'plugin::content-manager.explorer.delete', publish: 'plugin::content-manager.explorer.publish', unpublish: 'plugin::content-manager.explorer.publish', discard: 'plugin::content-manager.explorer.update', } as const;

To use the permission checker, retrieve it from the content-manager plugin: const permissionChecker = strapi .plugin('content-manager') .service('permission-checker') .create({ userAbility, model }); userAbility: The user's ability object containing their permissions. Accessed on the request context object: ctx.state.userAbility model: The content type model for which permissions are checked.

can.<action>()​ Determines if the user has permission to perform a specific action. if (permissionChecker.can.create()) { console.log('User can create content'); } cannot.<action>()​ Determines if the user does not have permission to perform a specific action. if (permissionChecker.cannot.delete()) { throw new errors.ForbiddenError('User is not allowed to delete content'); }

sanitizeOutput(data, { action })​ Cleans output data based on permissions. const sanitizedData = permissionChecker.sanitizeOutput(entity); sanitizeQuery(query, { action })​ Cleans a query before execution. const safeQuery = permissionChecker.sanitizeQuery({ page: '1', pageSize: '10' }); sanitizeInput(action, data, entity)​ Cleans input data before saving. const sanitizedInput = permissionChecker.sanitizeInput('create', inputData); sanitizeCreateInput(data)​ Shortcut for sanitizing create input. const sanitizedCreateData = permissionChecker.sanitizeCreateInput(inputData); sanitizeUpdateInput(entity) => (data)​ Shortcut for sanitizing update input. const sanitizedUpdateData = permissionChecker.sanitizeUpdateInput(existingEntity)(inputData);

validateQuery(query, { action })​ Ensures a query is valid based on permissions. const validatedQuery = permissionChecker.validateQuery({ page: '1', pageSize: '10' }); validateInput(action, data, entity)​ Ensures input data is valid before saving. permissionChecker.validateInput('update', inputData, existingEntity);
sanitizedQuery.<action>(query)​ Modifies queries to enforce permissions automatically. const securedQuery = permissionChecker.sanitizedQuery.read({ sort: 'createdAt:desc' });
export default ({ strapi }: { strapi: Core.Strapi }) => ({ create: createPermissionChecker(strapi), });
const canCreate = strapi.plugin('content-manager').service('permission-checker').can.create(); if (!canCreate) { throw new errors.ForbiddenError('User does not have permission to create content'); }

A release contains various content entries, each capable of being assigned a specific action such as publish or unpublish. Within a release, entries may be in different locales or come from different content types. With a simple click of a button, a release can execute the designated action for each entry. Content Releases is an enterprise edition feature. The plugin runs on the server and in the admin panel. The admin part plugs into the Content Manager edit view and list view. The server part depends on the Document Service to publish documents.

The plugin defines two hidden content types. Release (strapi_releases) stores the name, the status and the schedule. Release Action (strapi_release_actions) stores one action for one entry. An action links to its entry with contentType, locale and entryDocumentId, not with a relation, because the entry ID can change and the document ID does not. Read Backend design.

A release is planned until it runs, then frozen: nothing changes it afterwards. Planned statuses are recalculated on every change; frozen ones are written once. Empty (planned): the release has no entries. Ready (planned): publishing now would release every entry (all_or_nothing) or at least one (allow_partial). Blocked (planned): publishing now would release nothing, so it is refused. Done (frozen): every entry was released. A release with no entries ends done when it runs or misses its schedule. Partial (frozen, allow_partial only): some entries were released, the others skipped. Failed (frozen): the run released nothing, or a release with entries never ran before its date passed. One that failed before the upgrade is frozen as failed, empty or not, and may have released some entries: nothing recorded which. See Backend design for the rules behind each status.

A run holds the release row lock (forUpdate) for its whole transaction and rejects a release that already ran. It checks every publish entry before writing anything. A release that would release nothing is refused when published by hand, and frozen as failed when its schedule runs it. Otherwise, all_or_nothing releases every entry in one savepoint, so the first error rolls them all back and the release fails. allow_partial skips the entries that aren't publishable and releases each other entry in its own savepoint, so one that throws is skipped alone. The run records each entry's outcome and the release's totals, then freezes the release as done, partial or failed. Code: services/release.ts and services/release-run.ts.

The scheduling service adds one cron job per scheduled release with strapi.cron. At bootstrap, syncFromDatabase recreates the jobs for the releases that are not yet released. The row lock stops several instances from publishing the same release twice. Read Scheduling.

The plugin registers two Document Service middlewares, createDeleteActionsOnDelete and createRevalidateActionsOnDraftChange. It also subscribes to database lifecycles for deleteMany. Once the change commits, they remove the deleted entry's actions from planned releases or revalidate the changed draft, and recalculate the status of those releases. Handlers on the content type sync hooks remove the actions of a content type that is deleted or loses draft and publish, and revalidate the changed content types. See Extension points.
documents.s: Keeping actions in sync with documents

documents.t: Most EE features live in the EE folders of their package. Releases is built as its own plugin instead. The server entry checks strapi.ee.features.isEnabled('cms-content-releases'). When the feature is off, the plugin exports only register and contentTypes, so the release data stays in the database.

The admin part adds a menu link, a settings page, a dashboard widget and the Releases and Release details pages. It injects an edit view side panel, a document action, a bulk action and a list view column into the Content Manager through its plugin APIs and hooks. Read the frontend introduction and Content Manager and releases.

Enterprise Edition: how the license enables features such as cms-content-releases. Document write path: the publish calls that a release makes. Server lifecycle: where the plugin register and bootstrap run. @strapi/content-manager: hosts the edit view, list view and bulk action extension points. @strapi/admin: permissions, settings and the widget API. @strapi/core: Document Service, cron and webhook store. @strapi/data-transfer: skips the release content types during a transfer.
All backend code can be found in: packages/core/content-releases/server
The content-releases plugin creates two hidden content-types.

The Release content type stores all the information about a release and its associated Release Actions. It is saved in the database as strapi_releases. The schema can be found in: packages/core/content-releases/server/src/content-types/release/schema.ts releasedAt is when the release ran, or when the overdue sweep froze it without running (see Overdue releases). A release with releasedAt set is frozen: it can't be edited, deleted, published again or gain, lose or change entries, and it no longer counts as pending. Deleting is only for a planned release: a "Failed" one stays too (DELETE is refused with Release already published). On a "Failed" release nothing went live, except on one that failed before the upgrade, which may have released some entries.

Th Release Action content type is associated with any entry from any content-type that has draft and publish enabled. It is responsible for storing the action to perform for an associated entry. It is saved in the database as strapi_release_actions. In v4, we used built-in polymorphic relations, but for v5, we stored contentType, locale, and entryDocumentId in the Release Action schema to create a "manual" relationship between actions and entries. This approach allows us to link a release action to a document ID instead of a specific entry ID, as the entry ID may change over time and is not reliable. Only an action of a localized content type has a locale. The Content Manager sends the locale of its URL whatever the content type, so adding an action drops it for a content type that isn't localized, before the "already in the release" check: such an entry has one version, whatever the locale. Listing a release's actions (groupActions) also shows no locale for those content types, for actions stored before. The schema can be found in: packages/core/content-releases/server/src/content-types/release-action/schema.ts
Release and Release Action routes are only accessible on the Admin API.

Release routes can be found in: packages/core/content-releases/server/src/routes/release.ts Get all releases: method: GET endpoint: /content-releases/ params: { page: number; pageSize: number; // Any field of the release, e.g. filters[status][$in][0]=failed or // filters[scheduledAt][$null]=true filters?: Record<string, unknown>; sort?: string | string[]; // e.g. 'updatedAt:desc' } response meta: pagination, pendingReleasesCount (releases without releasedAt) and statusCounts (how many releases have each status, whatever the filters) a sort starting with scheduledAt lists the unscheduled releases first in either direction. Each database places nulls its own way, so findPage counts the unscheduled and scheduled releases matching the filters, then fills the page from the unscheduled ones first and the scheduled ones after. Ties, and the unscheduled releases, go most recently updated first, then by id. Get all releases with/without an entry: method: GET endpoint: /content-releases/getByDocumentAttached params: { contentType: string; locale?: string; entryDocumentId?: string; hasEntryAttached?: boolean; } Get a single release method: GET endpoint: /content-releases/:id Create a release: method: POST endpoint: /content-releases/ body: { name: string; scheduledAt?: string | null; // ISO date timezone?: string | null; // required when scheduledAt is set releaseCondition?: 'all_or_nothing' | 'allow_partial'; // all_or_nothing if omitted } Update a release: method: PUT endpoint: /content-releases/:id body: { name: string; scheduledAt?: string | null; // null or omitted unschedules the release timezone?: string | null; // required when scheduledAt is set; null or omitted clears it releaseCondition?: 'all_or_nothing' | 'allow_partial'; } Delete a release: method: DELETE endpoint: /content-releases/:id only a planned release (no releasedAt) can be deleted; one that ran, "Failed" included, is refused with a 400: Release already published Publish a release: method: POST endpoint: /content-releases/:id/publish Create a release from skipped entries: method: POST endpoint: /content-releases/:id/create-from-skipped-entries permissions: plugin::content-releases.create and plugin::content-releases.create-action response: the new release, with actions.meta.count body: { name: string; scheduledAt?: string | null; // ISO date timezone?: string | null; // required when scheduledAt is set releaseCondition?: 'all_or_nothing' | 'allow_partial'; actionIds?: number[]; // skipped entries to carry over; all of them if omitted, an empty array is a 400 }

Create a release action method: POST endpoint: /content-releases/:releaseId/actions body: { type: 'publish' | 'unpublish', contentType: string; locale?: string; entryDocumentId?: string; } Get release actions from a release method: GET endpoint: /content-releases/:releaseId/actions params: { page: number; pageSize: number; groupBy?: 'contentType' | 'action' | 'locale'; // ready / notReady: whether the entry is publishable (every unpublish is). On a release that // ran, that's what the run found. // released / skipped: what the run did with the entry. Nothing matches on a planned release. // blocking: skipped for a reason of its own (skipped_invalid, skipped_not_approved, // skipped_error), not held or missed: in an `all_or_nothing` run, what held back the rest. filter?: 'ready' | 'notReady' | 'released' | 'skipped' | 'blocking'; // Any field of the release action, narrowing the result further, e.g. // filters[outcome][$in][0]=skipped_invalid filters?: Record<string, unknown>; } each action has its entry, or null when the entry or its content type was deleted after the release ran Update a release action method: PUT endpoint: /content-releases/:releaseId/actions/:actionId body: { type: 'publish' | 'unpublish'; } Delete a release action method: DELETE endpoint: /content-releases/:releaseId/actions/:actionId
Handles requests to interact with the Release content type packages/core/content-releases/server/src/controllers/release.ts
Handles requests to interact with the Release Action content type
Interacts with the database for Release CRUD operations packages/core/content-releases/server/src/services/release.ts
Interacts with the database for Release Actions CRUD operations packages/core/content-releases/server/src/services/release-action.ts
Exposes validation functions to run before performing operations on a Release packages/core/content-releases/server/src/services/validation.ts

Exposes methods to schedule release date for releases. packages/core/content-releases/server/src/services/scheduling.ts Overdue releases​ syncFromDatabase arms future dates, and runs right away a release whose date passed by less than the grace period (the server was restarting when it was due): it uses the scheduled run's path (publish with trigger: 'scheduled', under the release lock), so with several instances booting together one runs it and the others find it already published. A release that comes due while the sync is still arming jobs runs right away too: cron never fires a job for a date already past, so the sync cancels that job. A release whose scheduled run didn't happen otherwise would stay in Pending with a past date. freezeOverdueReleases runs at bootstrap, before syncFromDatabase and with the same now, then every minute, and freezes these releases (releasedAt set) without running anything: a release whose scheduledAt is older than the grace period (OVERDUE_GRACE_PERIOD_MS, 5 minutes): the server was down, or the run was rolled back by a database error. failureReason is missed_schedule. It sends the releases.publish webhook (isPublished: false, an error named MissedSchedule) and a release.trigger audit failure attributed to the scheduler. A release with no entries missed nothing: it ends "Done" instead (totals all 0, failureReason null), with the success webhook and audit event its scheduled run would have sent. a release that failed before the upgrade: before failed runs were frozen, they left status: failed without releasedAt. It's frozen whatever its schedule, its job never armed. failureReason is failed_before_upgrade, and nothing is sent: it reported its failure then. It stays "Failed" even with no entries. Until the grace period has passed, an overdue release stays planned and can be published by hand: publishing late beats failing. The grace period also keeps the sweep from freezing a release its scheduled run is about to release. A manual publish doesn't check the schedule, on purpose. Every entry gets the outcome skipped_missed and keeps the validity last checked (nothing is checked at freeze time). The totals are 0 published, 0 unpublished, every entry skipped, so "Create release from skipped entries" carries over every entry of a release that missed its schedule. For failed_before_upgrade they don't say what went out: the old run stopped at its first error and kept the entries released before it, and nothing recorded which. Read them as unknown, not as skipped: the API returns skipped_missed and these totals, with only failureReason telling the two apart. "Create release from skipped entries" refuses such a release (the admin hides the button), so it doesn't publish entries again; otherwise it shows like one that missed its schedule. Each release is frozen in its own transaction, under a run's row lock, and checked again under it: a run in progress, or a reschedule to a later date, wins. It reads no entry, so it can't deadlock with a run. It throws inside another transaction, which would hold every lock until that one ends. A sweep that starts during another joins it; on a cluster, the lock lets one node freeze and report each release. A release that fails to freeze is left for the next sweep. On MySQL, a run still going 5 minutes after its date can make the sweep's lock wait time out (innodb_lock_wait_timeout): that's logged every minute until the run commits. failureReason is null on every release that ran, and on an empty release that missed its schedule, which the sweep froze as done; an empty failed_before_upgrade release keeps its failureReason and is frozen as failed.

Each release has a releaseCondition: all_or_nothing (the default, also given to releases created before the field existed) or allow_partial. A publish entry is publishable when its draft passes publish validation and, if its review workflow has a stage required to publish, it is at that stage. Unpublish entries are always publishable. Each release action stores whether its entry was publishable when last checked (isEntryValid) and, if not, why (reason, the shape a run records). The check reads the deep-populated draft, as a run does, so the stored reason matches what the run will decide. A draft that can't be read is stored as not publishable, with only the error's name, and its message if it's an ApplicationError (meant for the client; another error's message can carry row contents). Only planned releases are rewritten: a release that ran keeps what its run saw. The validity is written when an entry is added or changes type, when a manual publish is rejected by the check, and through revalidatePlannedActions when: the entry is edited or its draft discarded; a review workflow is created, updated or deleted; a content type's attributes change, at startup; at startup, for planned actions stored as not publishable before reasons existed (addReasonsToInvalidActions). revalidatePlannedActions reads the planned actions (PLANNED_ACTION_WHERE) and their drafts before taking any lock, each draft once however many releases the entry is in. Then it changes one release at a time, each in its own transaction under the release lock, and recalculates its status. A release that ran in between is left alone; one whose writes fail is logged without stopping the others. Each draft's updatedAt is read before the check and again under the lock: a draft saved in between is checked again under the lock, so a revalidation that started before a save never overwrites the result of the save's own, newer revalidation. Entry and workflow changes start it after their commit, without waiting (runAfterCommit), so their writes never wait on a release lock a run holds. The releases list and the single release response return actions.meta.notReadyCount for planned releases: the publish entries that aren't publishable now. With actions.meta.count and the release condition, it gives the status the other condition would have, so no per-condition status is stored. Empty: the release has no entries. Blocked: publishing now would release nothing. With all_or_nothing, at least one entry is not publishable. With allow_partial, no entry is publishable. Ready: otherwise. An allow_partial release with some entries that aren't publishable is ready: they are skipped when it runs. A release is planned (Empty, Ready, Blocked) until it runs. After it runs, it is frozen with one of these statuses, which nothing changes afterwards: Done: every entry was published or unpublished. A release with no entries ends done when it runs or misses its schedule; an empty release that failed before the upgrade ends failed. Partial: some entries were released and some were not. Failed: no entry was released. Considering that retrieving the status of all entries in a release is a heavy operation, we don't fetch it every time a user wants to access a release. Instead, we store the status in a field within the Release Content Type, and we only update it when an action that changes the status is triggered. These actions include: Creating a release:​ When creating a release, its status is automatically set to "Empty" as there are no entries initially. Creating a release from skipped entries:​ A release that ran can't change, so its skipped entries are released again through a new release: POST /content-releases/:id/create-from-skipped-entries. An entry is skipped when its outcome is neither published nor unpublished. Only a partial or failed release that ran is accepted. A release that hasn't run is rejected with Release not published yet, a done one with Release has no skipped entries, one that failed before the upgrade with Release failed before the upgrade, so its skipped entries are unknown (all 400). An unknown :id is a 404. The new release's fields are validated like any new release. actionIds restricts the entries to those actions; it must hold at least one id (an empty array is a 400, omit it to carry over every skipped entry), and an id that isn't a skipped entry of the release is a 400. Each entry keeps its type and locale, in the order it was added. Its validity is read from the entry as it is now, and the new release's status follows from it. Entries deleted since the run (in their locale, for a localized content type), or whose content type was deleted or lost Draft and Publish, are left out. If nothing is left, the request is rejected with a 400: Release has no skipped entries, or The requested entries can no longer be released when actionIds was given. The release, its entries and its status are written in one transaction. The source release isn't changed. Adding an entry to a release:​ Upon adding an entry to a release, its status is recalculated to either "Ready" or "Blocked" from the validity of its entries and its release condition. The recalculations below only apply to a planned release. updateReleaseStatus also leaves alone a failed release without releasedAt, which failed before the upgrade and is left for the overdue sweep. It reads the release under its row lock, so its counts are those of the last committed change and it can't overwrite a newer status. The stored validity has no such guarantee: two overlapping re-checks of an entry can leave the older draft's validity until the next one. Changing a release's entries through the API writes the change and the recalculated status in one transaction, under the release lock: if the recalculation fails, the change is rolled back, and a release that ran is refused (Release already published). Editing or deleting the release takes the same lock, so one frozen while the request was in flight is refused. Editing, discarding or deleting the entry recalculates in the background (see "Listening to events on entries"). Removing an entry from a release:​ After removing an entry from a release, the status is recalculated to determine if the release is now "Ready", "Blocked", or "Empty". Updating a release:​ Whenever a release is updated, its status is recalculated, so switching the release condition switches between "Ready" and "Blocked". The recalculation is awaited, so a read right after the update sees the new status. Publishing a release:​ A publish is either manual (the publish button or the API) or scheduled (the scheduler, at the release date). Under the release row lock, the run first reads every publish entry's current draft and checks whether it is publishable, before writing anything. A check that throws, whatever the error (e.g. its draft can't be read), isn't an entry validation result: the entry is recorded as skipped_error with isEntryValid: false, and isn't publishable. With api.documents.strictRelations, the check validates the draft as publish does: publish connects each relation to its target's published version and drops the targets without one, so a required relation counts only its targets that have a published version or that an earlier entry of the same run publishes (and not one an earlier entry unpublishes). It doesn't know whether that earlier entry will go out: if it doesn't, the entry fails when written, as below. A planned release's stored validity checks the draft as is, since which targets a run releases first is only known in the run. Entries are then handled one at a time: content types in relation dependency order, publishes before unpublishes, each in the order they were added. They share the lock transaction, and are written in savepoints (strapi.db.savepoint), so a failure rolls back exactly what it should. allow_partial: entries that aren't publishable are skipped without being written. Each other entry is published or unpublished in its own savepoint: if that throws, only that entry is rolled back and skipped, and the run moves on. The check can pass an entry that still fails when written, for example when an earlier entry of the same run takes its unique value: since a publish removes the entry's published version before it validates the new one, the savepoint is what keeps that version online. all_or_nothing: if any entry isn't publishable, no entry is written. Otherwise every entry is published or unpublished in one savepoint, and the first error rolls them all back. The run decides from this check, not from the stored status: a release that reads "Blocked" only because a background revalidation hasn't caught up with a fixed entry yet is published. When the check finds that a run would release nothing (all_or_nothing: any entry not publishable; allow_partial: no entry publishable; never for a release with no entries): A manual publish is rejected (400) with the first not-publishable entry's own error, in run order. When only checks that threw block it, the error is An entry couldn't be checked (<error name>), never the thrown message. Nothing is published, each check that ran is stored on the release actions (isEntryValid), and the status is recalculated, so the release stays planned and reads "Blocked" even if the stored values had gone out of date. A check that threw (e.g. a transient read error) found nothing about its entry: it isn't stored, the entry keeps the validity stored before. No webhook or audit event is sent. A scheduled run fails: the release is frozen as "Failed". For all_or_nothing, it records the first not-publishable entry's own error, or else the first thrown check's error; for allow_partial, No entries were published. Database caveats: A conflict with another transaction isn't the entry's own failure, so it isn't recorded as skipped_error: a MySQL deadlock (ER_LOCK_DEADLOCK, InnoDB rolls back the whole transaction, not the savepoint) or lock wait timeout (ER_LOCK_WAIT_TIMEOUT), a Postgres deadlock (40P01) or serialization failure (40001). Nor is a savepoint the database couldn't release or roll back to (SavepointError, see Database transactions), e.g. after a lock wait timeout with innodb_rollback_on_timeout rolled the whole transaction back. Under either mode, during the check or the writes, it rolls the whole run back, nothing is recorded, the release stays planned, and the request fails with a 500. A lock wait timeout is treated as a conflict whatever innodb_rollback_on_timeout says: with it off, InnoDB only rolls back the statement, but the entry still didn't fail on its own. An unexpected error that stops a manual all_or_nothing run is recorded as "Failed", and the request fails with a 400 that carries the frozen release in error.details.release: a validation error keeps its message and details; any error that isn't an ApplicationError becomes An entry couldn't be released (<error name>), never the thrown message, which is logged instead. Another ApplicationError is sent as is (its own status, no release). A run that rolls back (a conflict, a failed write of what it did) still fails with a 500. How a run ends: Every entry released, or no entries at all: "Done", with releasedAt set. Some entries released and some not (an allow_partial run that skipped entries): "Partial", with releasedAt set. No entry released (an allow_partial run whose entries all failed, or an all_or_nothing run stopped by an error): "Failed", with releasedAt set, and the request fails. A validation error (400) then carries the frozen release in error.details.release, which a refused publish never has. The release leaves Pending and can't be published again: its entries go out in a new release. A run either records its outcome or doesn't happen. Only the failures the run decides are recorded as "Failed" (a scheduled run stopped by the check, an all_or_nothing run stopped by an entry error, an allow_partial run where every entry failed). Any other error (reading the entries, writing the result, the writes of a rejected manual publish) rolls the whole transaction back, the entries it released included: the request fails, the release stays as it was, and no webhook or audit event is sent. A scheduled release whose run rolled back is frozen by the overdue sweep (see Scheduling); a manual one can be published again. Each entry of the run records what happened to it on its release action, returned by GET /content-releases/:releaseId/actions: outcome When reason published the entry was published null unpublished the entry's published version was removed, or the entry was already unpublished (its draft is there, with nothing to remove) null skipped_invalid the draft failed publish validation, whether or not it was also at the wrong stage, or publishing it raised a validation error (e.g. a unique clash with another entry of the run), or the entry is gone: a publish finds no draft, an unpublish finds neither a published version nor a draft (an all_or_nothing run fails on it) validation.errors: field path and message, without the error's value; a type-mismatch message loses the value it ends with; empty for an entry that's gone skipped_not_approved the entry wasn't at the stage required to publish, at the check or when review-workflows refused its publish stage: the entry's stage and the required one, read again after a refused publish (if that read fails, error with the refusal) skipped_error publishing or unpublishing the entry threw an error other than a validation error, or checking it threw any error error.name, and error.code for a database driver's error (e.g. 23505: node-postgres names its errors error); error.message too for an ApplicationError, never another error's message (it can carry row contents) skipped_held the entry was publishable, but an all_or_nothing run released nothing (at the check or after an error) null skipped_missed the release froze without running: its scheduled run never happened, or it failed before the upgrade (frozen by the overdue sweep, see Scheduling) unchanged: the validity last stored An entry that fails both checks keeps both in its reason. The outcomes are written in the lock transaction with the release's status, with the validity the run found: isEntryValid is false for skipped_invalid and skipped_not_approved, and true for every other outcome except a skipped_error entry whose check threw, so it never contradicts the outcome. A release runs once: its outcomes are never rewritten afterwards, a failed release included. A run that records nothing leaves outcome empty: a manual publish rejected by the check (it didn't run), and a run the database rolls back. The run also stores its totals on the release, with its status: totalPublishedEntries and totalUnpublishedEntries count the entries recorded as published and unpublished, and totalSkippedEntries every other entry of the run, whatever the reason (each entry keeps its own outcome and reason). The three always add up to the release's entries when it ran: a "Failed" release has 0 published and every entry skipped. GET /content-releases/:id and GET /content-releases return them on each release, and POST /content-releases/:id/publish returns them in its meta too, with totalEntries their sum. They stay null while the release is planned, including after a manual publish rejected by the check. The status written, the releases.publish webhook and the release.trigger audit event always agree. The webhook's release is the release as the run left it, with its totals, also when it failed: Status Webhook isPublished Audit outcome Audit details Done true success published, unpublished, failed: 0 Partial true partial published, unpublished, failed Failed false failure reason: the error's name The audit counts are the release's totals, failed being totalSkippedEntries: the entries the run left out, not publishable, or their publish or unpublish threw. The webhook and the audit event are sent once the outcome is committed. Entry errors are rolled back with their savepoint, so on Postgres they don't abort the transaction; any other error rolls back the whole run, as above. Listening to events on entries:​ When an entry is updated, its draft is discarded or it is deleted, the status of all releases containing that entry is recalculated to reflect any changes in validity. Only releases that haven't run are affected: an update or a discarded draft rewrites isEntryValid and reason (a discarded draft is replaced by the published version, for each locale it was discarded in) and a deletion removes the entry's actions only there. A release that ran keeps the actions of deleted entries, with what the run recorded; GET /content-releases/:releaseId/actions returns them with a null entry and status. This work isn't awaited by the entry's request (runAfterCommit) and runs outside its transaction, so the request responds before the releases' isEntryValid, reason and status change: a client that shows them right after a save must re-read them until they do. It starts once that transaction commits (right away without one). It reads the committed entry, can't undo the request's writes, and doesn't run for a change that was rolled back. Each affected release is then changed in a transaction of its own, under its lock. Failures are logged. On delete, createDeleteActionsOnDelete removes the actions of the locales the delete removed, resolved the way the Document Service resolves the locale param: every action of the document for a non-localized content type (their locale is stored as null) or for locale: '*', the given locale or locales otherwise, and the default locale when none is given.

These run on every content type sync. The revalidation passes aren't awaited by startup and log their failures. Before the sync: disableContentTypeLocalized (the actions of a content type that is no longer localized lose their locale). After the sync: deleteActionsOnDeleteContentType and deleteActionsOnDisableDraftAndPublish: the content type's actions leave every planned release. Releases that ran keep them; for a deleted content type, they're listed with a null entry and the uid as display name. They run after the sync because they recalculate statuses, which reads the current schema. enableContentTypeLocalized: the actions of a newly localized content type get the default locale. revalidateChangedContentTypes: the planned actions of content types whose attributes changed are revalidated. migrateIsValidAndStatusReleases: releases from before statuses existed get one. addReasonsToInvalidActions: see above. migrateReleaseConditionReleases: releases from before the condition existed get all_or_nothing. addOutcomesToReleasedReleases: a release that ran before outcomes existed released every entry (a failed run left it planned), so each action gets published or unpublished and the release its totals and the status done (an entry change used to recalculate a released release's status as if it were planned). A release a since-removed migration froze as failed_before_upgrade, without totals, gets every entry skipped_missed and all-skipped totals, as the sweep writes. Releases that failed before the upgrade are frozen by the overdue sweep at bootstrap (see Scheduling). addReasonsToInvalidActions finds again, at the next start, the actions of a release whose revalidation failed. revalidateChangedContentTypes doesn't: once the sync has stored the new schema, the attributes no longer differ, so a failed release keeps its stored validity until its entries change.

When entries are deleted outside the Document Service (afterDeleteMany, e.g. when a locale is deleted), their actions are deleted in releases that haven't run and those releases' status is recalculated, after the deletion commits, as in "Listening to events on entries".

There are two pages, ReleasesPage and ReleaseDetailsPage. To access these pages a user will need a valid Strapi license with the feature enabled and at least plugin::content-releases.read permissions. Redux toolkit is used to manage content releases data (data retrieval, release creation and editing, and fetching release actions). Formik is used to create/edit a release and all input components are controlled components.

Most licenses have feature-based usage limits configured through Chargebee. These limits are exposed to the frontend through useLicenseLimits. If the license doesn't specify the number of maximum pending releases a hard-coded default is used: max. 3 pending releases.
For a list of all available endpoints please refer to the detailed backend design documentation.

The release details page allows users with appropriate permissions to do the following: Group entries:​ Entries in a release can be grouped by the following options: Content-Types: Group all entries with the same content type together Locales: Group all entries with the same locale together. Actions: Group all entries with the same action (publish/unpublish) together. The tabs (All, Ready / Not ready or Released / Skipped) and the grouping live in the URL (filter, groupBy). Changing them replaces the current history entry, so Back leaves the page instead of stepping through the tabs. Edit a release:​ Until a release has run, a "three dot" button in the header gives access to a menu with an "Edit" option, enabled if the user has the plugin::content-releases.update permissions. The Edit option opens a side panel, enabling users to modify the release name, schedule and release mode. The name must be non-empty and unique among pending releases. Delete a release:​ The same menu has a "Delete" option, enabled if the user has the plugin::content-releases.delete permissions. Selecting it opens a confirmation modal. The menu only shows until the release runs: a release that ran, "Failed" included, can't be deleted. Create a release from skipped entries:​ Once a release has run as partial or failed (except a release that failed before the upgrade, which the API refuses too), a "Create release from skipped entries" button appears in the header. It requires the plugin::content-releases.create and plugin::content-releases.create-action permissions and is hidden when every skipped entry has since been deleted. It opens a side panel listing the entries carried over to the new release, with the release mode defaulting to "Release all ready items" and the date left empty: the user picks one or ticks "I don't have a release date yet". View Entry Status​ Each entry within a release shows a status badge (components/ReleaseActionStatus.tsx): In a planned release, "Ready" or "Not ready". An unpublish is always ready: nothing is checked. In a release that ran, "Done", "Skipped", or "Unknown" for a release that failed before the upgrade. In a release that ran, the action column shows the action as text, with an upload icon for a publish and a download icon for an unpublish, instead of the publish/unpublish segmented control. "Not ready" and "Skipped" open the reason drawer (components/EntryReasonDrawer.tsx). Its badge shows only the status ("Not ready" / "Skipped"), with the reason beside it ("Validation error"), or no reason when the entry has several kinds of issue (a failed field and a missing review stage, say). It lists the reason stored with the action (reason) in one box, under the number of issues, one card per issue: each field that failed, by a name built from its path and what's wrong in plain words (utils/fieldErrors.ts), the review stage the entry is missing, or the name of the error a run failed on, with its message when the server kept it (an ApplicationError's). A held or missed entry's card is the sentence that explains it. A held entry also lists, under "Held back by", the entries that held back its all_or_nothing run (the blocking filter, the first 5, then a count of the rest); each opens its own reason in the drawer. For a release that ran, a note dates the reasons: by the run, or by the schedule for one that froze without running (failureReason), with no date when that one had no schedule. The date reads as in the page header (getReleaseDateParts in utils/time.ts: the release's timezone, a 24-hour time and the UTC offset). A planned release's reasons are live, so it has no note. Previous and Next step through the entries that have a reason, in the table's order. The first 100 load, then twice as many each time more are needed: when Next is pressed on the last one loaded, or when the opened row isn't among them, up to 500. An opened row past the first 500 steps through the table's rows only. "Go to entry" opens the entry in the Content Manager with its validation errors shown, for a user allowed to read it. Next to the status, a button opens the reason drawer: it names the reason when the entry has a single one, "View details" otherwise, and its accessible name stays "Why {entry} isn't ready" / "Why {entry} was skipped". In a planned release, each row has its publish/unpublish action as a segmented control (components/ReleaseActionOptions.tsx, disabled without the update permission) and, revealed on row hover or keyboard focus, an eye icon that opens the entry and a "Remove from release" icon (ReleaseActionMenu.DeleteReleaseActionButton). In a release that ran, the eye icon is the row's only action, as there's nothing to remove. The eye shows for a user who can read the entry's content type, in the action's locale for a localized one. Within the CM edit view, users can resolve any identified errors. Saving, publishing or unpublishing the entry there refetches the release, so its status is up to date when the user comes back; the "Refresh" button re-checks every entry on demand. Publish a release:​ To execute the release of a content release, users can simply click on the "Publish" button (shown if you have the "plugin::content-releases.publish" permission). It's disabled while the release is empty or blocked, as running it would release nothing; a tooltip on it, reachable from the keyboard, says why ("This release is empty.", or for a blocked release what its release mode needs). A release that reads ready may still be refused if an entry changed since it was checked: the notification shows why, and the release reads blocked after the refetch. The notification after a run follows its outcome: a success when every entry was released, a warning with the counts ("Released 8 of 10 entries, 2 skipped") for a partial run, and a danger notification saying nothing was released, with the run's error, for a failed run (the API answers with the frozen release in the error's details, which tells it from a refused publish). For a failed all_or_nothing run, the page first asks for the run's blocking entries and names the first ("Nothing was released, held back by Partner feed 1: …"); without one, e.g. a run that failed outside any entry, the notification names none. Header:​ The header subtitle joins its parts with " • ". A planned release shows its number of entries and, if scheduled, "Scheduled for {date}". A release that ran shows "Released on {date}" (its releasedAt, in the release's timezone or the browser's when unscheduled), then what the run released and skipped. A run that released nothing (every entry skipped) shows "Ran on {date} • Nothing was released • N skipped" instead. A release that missed its schedule or failed before the upgrade never ran: it shows its scheduled time, never the time it was frozen, and no date when it wasn't scheduled. One that missed its schedule then reads "Nothing was released • N skipped", never "Released 0 of N entries".

The releases page lists every release in one paginated table (10, 20, 50 or 100 per page, the admin's sizes; 10 by default), sorted by scheduled date (the unscheduled releases first, most recently updated first, then soonest first). Its columns are name, status, schedule, entries and release mode; clicking a row opens the release details page. The header subtitle shows the number of releases matching the applied filters (every release without filters). The schedule column shows the release's scheduledAt, the date the schedule sorts and the "Scheduled for" filter use, or "Not scheduled": a release published by hand without a schedule stays "Not scheduled" after it ran. Before the date, on the same line, the same instant reads as a relative time alone, sentence-cased ("In 2 days", "3 days ago", "Yesterday"), with no words around it: the status column tells a release that ran from one that missed its schedule, and the release details page shows when a release ran (releasedAt; for one that froze without running, failureReason set, releasedAt is only when it froze). The relative time counts days by calendar day in the viewer's timezone, not by elapsed 24-hour periods. A calendar icon marks a date still to come on a release that hasn't run and a paper plane any other date; "Not scheduled" has a minus icon. A release still to come (not run, and scheduled in the future or not at all) is in the table's text colour (neutral800) in its name, entries and release mode columns; a release that ran or whose schedule passed is grey (neutral600), so the runs to come stand out. The date itself is in the text colour only while it is still to come. The list, the release details and its entries refetch when content changes in the Content Manager (save, discard, delete, publish and unpublish, one entry or many: ENTRY_MUTATIONS in services/release.ts) and when an entry's review stage or a review workflow changes, as these change which entries are ready. The review-workflows mutations invalidate the ReviewWorkflowStages tag, which the release queries provide: extending those mutations from services/release.ts would depend on the plugins' load order. Filters​ A "Filters" button above the table opens the admin's list filters popover (Filters from @strapi/admin), with four fields: Status: the release's stored status (is / is not). Release mode: allow_partial or all_or_nothing (is / is not). Scheduled for: the release's scheduledAt. "Not scheduled" is is null. Released on: the release's releasedAt, set when it ran. "Not released yet" is is null. The two date fields use ScheduleFilterInput: a date, and an optional time. A date alone is stored in the URL as YYYY-MM-DD and matches that whole day; a date and a time is stored as an ISO string and matches that minute. Stored dates have seconds and milliseconds, so utils/scheduleFilters turns each date filter into bounds before calling the API: is becomes $gte start and $lt end, is not an $or outside them, and before/after the matching bound. Days and times are the viewer's, as in the pickers, and the time picker shows times in the admin locale's format. A hand-edited URL setting several operators on one date filter keeps all of them, combined with $and; a date that doesn't exist (e.g. 2026-13-45) is sent as it is. The date tags show the value through the filter's formatValue; the status and release mode tags show the option's label. Filters live in the URL as filters[$and], like the Content Manager list view, and combine with each other. Applied filters show as removable tags; "Clear all" next to the tags, or "Clear filters" in the empty state, removes them all. A filters[releasedAt] left in the URL by the old Pending/Done tabs is ignored, and so is a filters[$and] that isn't a list. Sort​ A "Sort" menu on the right of the filter bar sets the sort URL param: scheduled date soonest first (scheduledAt:asc, the default) or latest first (scheduledAt:desc), most recent updates, oldest updates, most recently created, and name A to Z or Z to A. Both schedule sorts list the unscheduled releases first, whatever the database (see the backend page). They sort by scheduledAt, the date the schedule column shows. Changing the sort keeps the applied filters and goes back to the first page; adding or clearing filters and changing page keep the sort. A sort set in the URL that the menu doesn't offer is still sent to the API; the menu then reads just "Sort". New Release Creation:​ If a user has the plugin::content-releases.create permission, a 'New release' button will be visible in the header. Clicking the button opens a side panel with the release name, its schedule ("I don't have a release date yet", then the date, time and timezone) and its release mode. The schedule uses the design system's DatePicker, TimePicker and Combobox: a combined date, time and timezone picker waits for the /next Popover, Calendar and Combobox (strapi/design-system#2082), so the plugin doesn't depend on @base-ui/react itself. The side panel reads a release's schedule as the date and time a clock in the release's timezone shows (getWallClock in utils/time.ts), never through a browser Date, so a time in the browser's DST gap doesn't shift. The form keeps the time as HH:mm; the time picker shows and returns it in the admin locale's format (10.00 in Finnish), as in the date filters. The date and time start empty. Ticking "I don't have a release date yet", which sits above the date and time so it doesn't move when they hide, only hides the schedule: unticking it brings back what was picked, and while it's ticked the schedule is neither validated nor submitted. The release modes list "Release all ready items" first and the default, "Require every entry to be ready", second (the reverse of RELEASE_CONDITIONS). The name of a pending release must be unique. Once created, the user is taken to the new release. If the API refuses it, e.g. for a name already in use, its error message shows in the notification. License limits​ If the user reaches the limit of maximum pending releases defined on their license then the 'New release' button is disabled and a banner is displayed to inform the user.

caution Content Releases Scheduling is not yet a stable feature. Therefore, all the elements documented on this page are not currently visible. If you wish to try Releases Scheduling, you can enable it at your own risk using the contentReleasesScheduling feature flag. Scheduling provides users with the ability to set a scheduled date for the release, automating its publication or unpublishing. When this happens, a webhook is triggered, providing the result of the attempt to publish the release.

Every time you create or update a release and add a scheduled date, the server responsible for handling this request will generate a new cronjob (via strapi.cron / croner) for the selected date to publish the release.

When selecting a scheduled date, you have the option to choose a specific timezone; by default, your system timezone is selected. This measure is taken to prevent any potential confusion when selecting the publication time for a release. Consequently, if a user sets a schedule for 16:00 using the "Europe/Paris" timezone (UTC+01:00), another user accessing the same release will see the same time (16:00 (UTC+01:00)), regardless of their system's timezone.

It's possible that your Strapi project runs on multiple instances. In such cases, what happens with the cronjobs? Do they all run simultaneously, attempting to publish the release multiple times? To understand how we address this scenario, it's important to differentiate between two cases when scheduling a release:
documents.s: Scheduling in a architecture with multiple Strapi instances

documents.t: If you have 3 Strapi instances running concurrently, and you distribute traffic among them using any method, there is not a big problem. This is because the server responsible for handling one request to create/update a release and add a schedule will be the only server with the associated cronjob. Then, there's no duplication, and potential race condition problems are avoided.

The problem is starting a new Strapi instance, because we retrieve all scheduled releases and ensure that cronjobs are created for each one. Consequently, multiple Strapi instances might end up with the same cronjob for a release publish. To address this, we implement the following logic: We set up a transaction that locks the release being published using SQL forUpdate. This means that any other processes attempting to access the release row will be put on hold until the first one finishes executing.
